title: Ensembling or not? On the value of boosting and bagging for physics-aware machine learning in hydrology
abstract: • Ensembling adds limited value to physics-aware Machine Learning (PaML) models. • Single well-configured PaML matches ensemble performance • Classical boosting compensates low-capacity PaML learners. • Bagging provides limited additional predictive benefit. • GrowNet-inspired boosting shows non-monotonic behavior. Ensemble machine learning methods such as bagging and boosting are widely used to improve predictive performance in hydrological modeling. However, their value when applied to physics-aware machine learning (PaML) models remains largely unexplored. This study investigates whether ensemble strategies provide tangible predictive gains over a standalone PaML model for streamflow simulation. Four controlled experiments were conducted on five representative catchments from the Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies dataset for the contiguous United States (CAMELS-US) to evaluate the influence of training epochs, base learner capacity, ensemble size, and training data length. Bagging, classical boosting, and a growth-based boosting formulation inspired by GrowNet were compared against both weak and well-configured single PaML models. Predictive performance was assessed using the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), the Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) and the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE). Results show that ensemble strategies do not yield substantial improvements over a properly configured standalone PaML model, despite requiring greater computational resources. While classical boosting can compensate for intentionally reduced model capacity by aggregating low-capacity PaML learners, the resulting gains remain marginal relative to a moderately expressive single model. Bagging provides limited additional benefits, and the growth-based boosting formulation exhibits non-monotonic and basin-dependent behavior. Overall, the findings suggest that, within the investigated framework, refining the architecture and capacity of a single PaML model is generally more effective than adopting ensemble strategies. These results contribute to clarifying the practical role of ensemble learning in physics-aware hydrological modeling.

title: Regional landslide early warning through machine-learning-based rainfall threshold and hydromorphological slope units
abstract: Regional landslide early warning (LEW) remains a fundamental challenge because of the spatial heterogeneity of hydrological–geomorphological units and the nonlinear responses inherent in rainfall-triggering processes. This study develops an integrated LEW framework that combines landslide susceptibility prediction (LSP) with rainfall-threshold modeling based on machine learning (ML) to advance the quantitative characterization of regional-scale rainfall-landslide hydrology. For spatial characterization, we propose a novel LSP model that integrates hydrological analysis (HA) and multi-scale segmentation (MSS) to better represent hydromorphological controls on the spatial distribution of slope failures. The HA–MSS model demonstrates strong spatial discriminability: “very high susceptibility” zones capture 69.33 % of observed landslides while occupying only 6.76 % of the total area. For temporal prediction, an ML-based rainfall-threshold model trained jointly on triggering and non-triggering events achieves a probability of detection of 0.82, an accuracy of 0.85, a probability of false detection of 0.13, and a Hanssen–Kuipers index of 0.69, substantially outperforming the empirical E–D baseline. Feature-importance analysis identifies event cumulative rainfall (ECR), maximum intensity (Imax), intensity (I), and duration (D) as dominant predictors, whereas antecedent rainfall variables (AR3, AR5, AR7) contribute 35.2 % of the total feature importance, highlighting the importance of antecedent wetness conditions in rainfall-induced landslide triggering. The integrated framework supports dynamic warning updates at hourly resolution through a spatiotemporal warning matrix. Retrospective assessment of the integrated LEW showed that approximately 87 % of historical landslides were associated with red or orange alert levels, while the August 2021 hindcast reproduced the temporal escalation and spatial evolution of warning levels during an intense rainfall event.

title: Improving flood forecasts: the combined impact of data assimilation and machine learning post-processing
abstract: Accurate streamflow forecasts are essential for flood risk management and impact mitigation. Coupling hydrological models with machine learning techniques has gained increasing attention as a means to improve forecast skill, with post-processing emerging as a promising approach to correcting systematic model residuals. However, the interaction between machine-learning post-processing, data assimilation and calibration strategies remains insufficiently explored. In this study, we assess the contribution of machine-learning-based post-processing to hourly streamflow forecasts for 687 catchments in metropolitan France, generated using a GR-family hydrological model (GR5H-RI) under three forecasting approaches differing in calibration strategy and use of data assimilation. Random Forest and Multilayer Perceptron models are used to post-process forecasts at lead times of 3, 6, 12 and 24 h. Forecast performance is evaluated using both continuous skill metrics relative to persistence and threshold-based metrics for flood event detection. Results show that (1) post-processing consistently improves forecast skill at short lead times, especially for slower-response catchments, with the median persistence score increasing from 0.33 to 0.54 at a 3-h lead time in the highest-skill forecasting setup and performance improving in 89.7% of catchments; (2) the largest gains occur for forecasts without data assimilation, suggesting that post-processing can partially compensate for the lack of state updating but cannot fully replace it; and (3) neural network-based post-processing slightly outperforms tree-based models in continuous metrics, while differences are more limited for event detection. Overall, results highlight the complementary roles of data assimilation and machine-learning post-processing and demonstrate the potential of such frameworks for operational flood forecasting.

title: Toward AI-driven digital twins for metropolitan floods: A conditional latent dynamics network surrogate of the shallow water equations
abstract: AI-driven flood digital twins demand fast hydrodynamic surrogates for ensemble forecasting and observation assimilation. Yet even GPU-accelerated two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers still require minutes per -hour run on a -million-active-cell metropolitan basin (the Des Plaines River basin at resolution), making such workloads prohibitive at native resolution. We present the Conditional Latent Dynamics Network (CLDNet): a low-dimensional latent neural ODE driven by rainfall, paired with a coordinate-based decoder conditioned on static terrain (elevation, slope, Manning roughness) that reconstructs depth and discharge at arbitrary query points. Pointwise decoding decouples memory from grid size and handles irregular watersheds natively, enabling metropolitan-scale training on a single compute node and direct queries at exact gauge coordinates without raster snapping. We evaluate CLDNet on a synthetic -cell Texas benchmark and on a new Des Plaines case study of real-rainfall Stage IV storms whose reference simulator we validate against United States Geological Survey (USGS) gauges at the April 2013 flood-of-record (Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency on mean-recentered water-surface elevation). CLDNet reduces the relative root-mean-squared error of an unconditional baseline by , outperforms regular-grid VAE–ConvLSTM and FNO baselines on the Texas benchmark (both presuppose a Cartesian grid and do not apply to the irregular Des Plaines watershed), reaches a critical success index of at the inundation threshold, and produces a full -hour basin-wide forecast in seconds—a speedup. Finally, we demonstrate that CLDNet’s compact latent state supports online observation coupling: using the Latent Dynamics Ensemble Score Filter (LD-EnSF), we assimilate water-depth observations at gauge locations into the surrogate’s latent dynamics and recover a mean Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency of against USGS observations at six held-out gauges, from for the rainfall-perturbed open-loop forecast, realizing the observation-update step required of an AI-driven flood digital twin.

title: AnytimeHydroTwin: A deployment-valid inference-orchestration layer for AI-driven hydrological digital twins
abstract: When does a water-quality nowcast need a process-resolving model, and when is the previous observation enough? Across eleven regimes on three tidal-estuarine systems, the answer is set by the signal, not the model. Estuarine pH and dissolved oxygen are persistence-dominated everywhere (lag-1 autocorrelation – ): a high-fidelity (HF) neural nowcaster beats the previous observation in none of the nine such regimes. Only Sacramento Delta 15-min turbidity genuinely decorrelates ( ), reflecting episodic sediment resuspension, and it alone rewards HF ( ). Variability is not the discriminant—the two highest-variance regimes are persistence-dominated—giving an operational screen: above , an expensive nowcaster will not repay its compute. We exploit this with AnytimeHydroTwin , an inference-orchestration layer rather than a full digital twin, whose deployment-valid pre-HF causal gate reads only observations available before the HF forward pass, so a skipped HF call is a real compute saving, not a post-hoc blend ratio. The gate is itself paid every step: an HF-invocation rate is not a compute saving, and we account for it in full. Our headline is a leakage-clean nested-split evaluation on Sacramento turbidity—NSE parity with HF-only, at HF, an estimated to end-to-end wall-clock saving from measured component latencies—closed for the two LSTM headline regimes, open for the TCN stress case and ancillary CAMELS variant. On the nine persistence-dominated regimes it safely defers to lag-1 of the time. This regime classification is robust across the three backbone families we evaluate (TCN, LSTM and Transformer): the structure reflects the signal more than the learner.

title: Deep learning with upstream-aware terrain representations and rainfall adapter for generalizable pluvial flood prediction
abstract: Deep learning-based surrogate models can substantially accelerate pluvial flood simulations. However, most existing approaches struggle to generalize across heterogeneous terrains or modified topographies, limiting their applicability for real-world flood risk assessment unless retrained for each specific terrain.In this work, we investigate how deep learning flood surrogates can be designed to achieve robust spatial generalization across previously unseen terrain configurations without retraining. We train models on diverse terrain and introduce upstream-aware input maps that propagate terrain properties into downstream regions, allowing the model to capture long-range spatial dependencies and supporting the learning of more generalizable spatial features. In addition, we add architectural design choices to improve the model’s capacity to generalize beyond the training domain. We further propose a two-stage training strategy with an adapter-like rainfall encoder that enables efficient adaptation to previously unseen rainfall intensities while preserving spatial generalizability.The resulting model predicts maximum water depths and is evaluated on unseen catchments in Austria and Denmark, as well as on artificially modified terrains such as dikes. Our results demonstrate that combining a large training dataset with upstream-aware terrain representations and a generalization-oriented architectural design enables accurate flood predictions across unseen terrains and rainfall scenarios, reaching a RMSE below $0.05$ and CSI$_{0.3}$ of up to $0.91$ in test cases, outperforming previous models in both prediction accuracy and Critical Success Index.

title: Hydrologically constrained genetic programming for interpretable rainfall–runoff model discovery: A process–informed machine learning approach
abstract: Advances in machine learning have improved rainfall–runoff prediction, but integrating these capabilities with interpretable, process-based model structures remains an open challenge. This study seeks a middle ground between conceptual hydrological modelling and modern data-driven prediction by automating model structure discovery while retaining interpretability and hydrological consistency. We introduce HydroXGP (Hydrological Model eXplorer using Genetic Programming) to reduce reliance on legacy model choices and subjective a priori structural assumptions by learning model structure directly from data during optimization. The framework evolves models from a modular, process-based component library adapted from the open-source MARRMoT toolbox, making the search process-informed through reusable flux and routing components and hydrologically constrained by enforcing mass balance during simulation. GP jointly optimizes model structure and parameters, while each discovered model remains explicit and interpretable. Evaluation on the CAMELS-US dataset showed that a proof-of-concept test in a snow-dominated basin achieved strong performance over the out-of-sample test period (NSE=0.849), and, when transferred to a hydrologically similar basin, the learned structure retained useful predictive skill (NSE=0.724). Across 18 basins (one representative basin per U.S. hydrologic region), median NSE reached 0.702, generally outperforming the mean performance of an ensemble of conceptual benchmark models while remaining competitive with some regional LSTM baselines. The findings support a modelling perspective in which structural hypotheses can be revisited and adapted as new data, diagnostics, or environmental signals become available, enabling basin-specific configurations that evolve in response to changing information rather than relying on a single fixed template.

title: Hybrid physics–AI modeling in hydrogeology: a review of concepts, applications, and challenges
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping hydrogeological modeling. The question is whether hybrid physics–AI approaches can reconcile the explanatory power of process-based models with the flexibility and speed of machine learning. We try to answer this question with a concept-driven review which traces the progression from purely data-driven approaches to emerging modeling paradigms incorporating physical knowledge. We show that hydrogeological modeling is moving beyond a simple opposition between mechanistic simulators and black-box algorithms toward a continuum of physics–AI integration, including theory-guided machine learning, physics-informed neural networks, physics-aware architectures, neural operators, generative models, and differentiable programming. Applications across key hydrogeological domains are reviewed, followed by a discussion of current limitations and barriers to operational deployment, including data requirements, transferability across hydrogeological settings, verification and validation, uncertainty quantification, and issues of trust. We conclude that hybrid physics–AI modeling should not be understood as a replacement for hydrogeological theory, but as an emerging methodological framework in which physical laws, numerical simulation, and machine learning are combined to produce models that are faster, more interpretable, more robust, and more useful for decision-making in groundwater science and management.

title: Deep learning meets spectral analysis: reproducing long-term persistence in synthetic streamflow
abstract: Synthetic streamflow generation requires simultaneous reproduction of flow distributions and temporal dependence across multiple scales, including long-term persistence (LTP). This study evaluates a three-stage framework that combines latent-space generation with a temporal convolutional network (TCN), low-frequency spectral adjustment, and quantile-based rank reordering. The framework was applied to daily discharge records from 24 UK river basins and benchmarked against autoregressive moving average (ARMA), k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN), and long short-term memory (LSTM) generators. Marginal distributions were reproduced closely (median Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic = 0.00069; 99th-percentile ratios = 0.986–0.999). The median absolute difference in the rescaled-range persistence estimate was 0.028, with 79% of basins within a tolerance of 0.05. Detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) produced a median scaling-exponent difference of 0.076; Monte Carlo tests showed that part of the R/S-DFA discrepancy reflects estimator-specific finite-sample behavior. The same experiments indicate that a 0.05 tolerance is approximately a two-standard-deviation band at the 7,300-day synthetic-series length, and that shorter records tend to inflate persistence estimates. ARMA produced a statistically indistinguishable median R/S error (0.024). For the nine records with no missing days, the proposed framework and k-NN showed very similar paired low-flow spell-duration errors. The proposed framework is therefore not uniformly superior to simpler alternatives; its main value is the combination of close marginal matching with an explicit spectral mechanism for controlling long-term persistence. Remaining limitations include weaker short-lag autocorrelation reproduction and incomplete recovery of threshold-conditioned spell clustering.

title: A large-scale molecular dynamics investigation of anisotropic hydraulic conductivity in compacted clay system
abstract: This study developed a large-scale molecular dynamics framework to investigate anisotropic hydraulic conductivity by linking directional water transport to compaction state, platelet fabric, and surface chemistry. A total of 150 multi-particle nanoflow models were constructed across dry densities ( ρ d ) of 1.2–1.8 g·cm −3 , orientational order parameters ( S ) of 0.60 to 0.92, and cation exchange capacities (CEC) of 0.11–97.44 cmol·kg −1 . Simulated hydraulic conductivities ranged from 0.77 × 10 -14 to 1.96 × 10 -12 m·s −1 , with 97.0% of available experimental measurements falling within this envelope. Mean horizontal hydraulic conductivity ( k h ) consistently exceeded mean vertical hydraulic conductivity ( k v ) by factors of approximately 2.4–5.6. Increasing dry density narrowed water-accessible pores, reduced independent spanning pathways and critical spanning diameters, and increased tortuosity, thereby decreasing both k h and k v . Platelet orientation differentiated the two flow directions by maintaining more direct horizontal pathways. Increasing CEC shifted pore water toward Na associated states and reduced the flux carried by interfacial only and free water, further lowering both k h and k v . Random Forest models achieved mean testing R 2 values of 0.92 for k h and 0.88 for k v and identified dry density as the dominant descriptor in both directions. Platelet orientation had a greater relative influence on vertical than horizontal conductivity, whereas CEC made a smaller but consistent contribution. Fixed-density sensitivity analysis showed that increasing dry density shifted the relative sensitivity weight from platelet orientation toward CEC, particularly for k v . These findings clarify the distinct structural and physicochemical controls on directional water transport and hydraulic anisotropy in compacted clay barriers.

title: A prototype multi-hazard early warning system integrating flood and landslide forecasting: application in the upper Garonne River Basin
abstract: Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems (MHEWS) are essential for disaster risk management, yet operational implementation remains limited by challenges in hazard integration, forecast uncertainty, and computational requirements. This study develops and evaluates a fast and lightweight prototype MHEWS integrating fluvial flooding and shallow landslide forecasting. The MHEWS couples snow-hydrological modeling (SNOW-17 and CREST) with a slope stability approach (infinite slope and Random Forest models) driven by bias-corrected Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) meteorological forecasts. Quantile mapping bias correction substantially improves precipitation and temperature forecast performance, reducing variability errors and enhancing distributional agreement. Applied in the Upper Garonne River Basin (Spanish Pyrenees) using 24-hour lead time forecasts, multi-hazard analysis for 2010–2020 reveals asymmetric coupling between hazards: flood warnings respond rapidly to rainfall intensity, while landslide warnings depend on cumulative subsurface conditioning and antecedent soil moisture, with high-level warnings rarely coinciding. Evaluation of multiple forecast lead times (24, 48, 72 h) for June 2013 demonstrates systematic performance degradation with increasing lead time, reflecting amplified uncertainty propagation. This degradation is further compounded by the limitations of the quantile mapping approach; while it effectively aligns marginal statistics, it fails to preserve temporal autocorrelation or event persistence. This introduces residual biases in cumulative dynamics that disproportionately affect landslide prediction compared to flood estimation. The fully automated prototype, designed to be scalable and transferable, and built on open-source software and cloud infrastructure, demonstrates operational feasibility for real-time early warning applications across hydro-meteorologically complex environments.

title: Streamflow prediction in natural ungauged catchments using Temporal Fusion Transformers
abstract: Streamflow prediction is essential for water resources management. Classical hydrological models struggle with predictive accuracy and probabilistic representation in ungauged catchments. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated notable improvements in reproducing complex time series, such as streamflow, with the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) emerging as a promising model. This study explores the potential of TFTs to predict daily streamflow in natural ungauged catchments in Portugal. Streamflow data from 53 catchments were collected from the national database, while meteorological inputs (precipitation and temperature) were derived from the ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset. Geomorphological descriptors for each catchment were also included. Results are reported on 46 catchments after screening from the initial set based on objective hydrometric and natural-flow criteria and show strong predictive performance and spatial generalization under ungauged conditions. In the test subsets, TFT models in ungauged conditions outperformed individually calibrated hydrological models Hydrologiska Byråns Vattenbalansavdelning (HBV), securing advantage in terms of median NSE (increased from 0.46 to 0.50), median KGE (increased from 0.44 to 0.48) and median CRPS (decreased, which is desired, from 5.51 to 3.75 ). Model specialization significantly improved performance, reaching a median NSE = 0.62, a median KGE = 0.65, and the median CRPS decreases to 3.20 , in selected test portions for this second task. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models were also evaluated as a data-driven benchmark, with TFTs achieving competitive performance under ungauged conditions. Additionally, retraining experiments highlight the model’s adaptability, showing that local data, even if limited in number, can be instrumental in further improving predictions. These findings support the application of deep learning in operational settings, such as flood and drought risk management, and water allocation strategies in catchments without comprehensive measurements.

title: Global patterns of reservoir normal water storage capacities estimated by statistical and machine learning models
abstract: Reservoir water storages are increasingly recognized as important tools for adapting to water-related hazards under climate change, particularly through their normal water storage (NWS). However, a critical data gap on regarding global reservoir NWS hinders our understanding of their spatial patterns and impacts on water management. This study aims to bridge this data gap by estimating the NWS for 7,250 global reservoirs using an ensemble approach that includes linear regression, machine learning, and satellite-based methods. We train and evaluate these models based on a representative sample of 801 reservoirs with reported NWS data and multiple static attributes. Among the evaluated methods, the Gradient Boosted Decision Trees model utilizing various reservoir features performed best (achieving a coefficient of determination of 0.95 and a mean absolute percentage error of 12%), and was subsequently selected to estimate the NWS for unrecorded reservoirs. Our analysis of the global reservoir NWS ratio (NWSR) at individual, basin, and national scales reveals significant spatial variations, with a global mean NWSR of 72%. The distribution of NWSRs varies considerably across different reservoir groups categorized by physical size, primary purpose, and climatic region. At the national and basin scales, the USA, Canada, China, Russia, and Brazil, along with the Yenisey, Nile, Mississippi, Parana, and Yangtze basins, account for substantial portions of the global NWS capacity. The developed dataset and the analyzed spatial patterns provide vital empirical inputs for water resource management, large-scale hydrological modeling, and climate change adaptation, ultimately supporting effective planning for sustainable freshwater supplies.

title: Effects of droughts and warm months on phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations in surface waters globally
abstract: Phosphorus (P) and nitrogen (N) concentrations in surface waters are substantially affected by droughts and warm months. However, previous studies of phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations under these hydro-climatic extremes are limited to a small number of regions, mainly in parts of North America, Europe and Australia. Here we perform the first global-scale analysis of phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations in surface waters under droughts, warm months and compound drought-warm months for the period 1980–2010. To achieve this, we developed an approach to downscale existing simulation data of total phosphorus (TP) and total nitrogen (TN) concentrations from annual to monthly level with machine learning at 0.5 × 0.5 degree resolution. The results indicate generally mixed responses in phosphorus and nitrogen concentrations under drought, with some regions showing increases in the concentrations of phosphorus and nitrogen due to drought and others showing decreases. Additionally, the results show more consistent increases in phosphorus (P) concentrations during warm months (average change: +21%) and compound drought-warm months (average change: +10%), which was mainly attributed to less dilution during periods of low flow and high temperature. Furthermore, there is a general decrease in the N:P ratio observed globally during warm months (average change: −11%). The results from this study provide a broader understanding of the effects of droughts and warm months on phosphorus and nitrogen in surface waters compared to previous local-scale studies. Furthermore, the results highlight the significant changes in phosphorus and nitrogen ratios during droughts and warm months, which may significantly influence freshwater ecosystem health worldwide.

title: High-frequency monitoring and reconstruction of lake water temperature with meteorological observations
abstract: Lakes, as vital components of land water systems, play crucial roles in local climate regulation and ecological functions. Water temperature is a key indicator of lake thermal dynamics and climate sensitivity, while its high-frequency variations and coupling mechanisms with meteorological drivers remain insufficiently understood, especially under extreme weather conditions. To bridge this gap, we conducted a detailed investigation of Qinghai Lake using high-resolution (1 h interval) observations of water temperature and meteorological variables from October 2023 to October 2024. We developed a comprehensive analytical framework incorporating statistical analysis, wavelet time–frequency decomposition, anomaly detection, and deep learning-based reconstruction. The results reveal a strong nonlinear relationship between water and air temperature, as demonstrated by RAPS trend analysis and S-curve regression (R2 = 0.82). Wavelet coherence analysis indicates robust coupling at diurnal and synoptic timescales, with a distinct temporal lag in the lake’s thermal response to atmospheric forcing. Anomaly detection further highlights the critical role of strong wind and precipitation in driving abrupt water temperature shifts. To improve reconstruction performance, we propose a novel PCA-GRU-MA model, which integrates Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), and Multi-Head Attention mechanisms (MA). Model validation demonstrates superior accuracy compared to seven benchmark models (RMSE = 1.55 °C, MAE = 1.15 °C, NSE = 0.94), underscoring its capacity to capture thermal anomalies and effectiveness in reconstructing hourly water temperature. This study advances the understanding of high-resolution lake thermal dynamics and offers a methodological foundation for lake ecosystem management, climate change adaptation, and early-warning systems.

title: Hydrogeological controls on seasonal groundwater level dynamics across Greece: A national-scale assessment integrating monitoring data, earth observation, and interpretable machine learning (2013–2022)
abstract: Groundwater monitoring networks typically provide broad spatial coverage but sparse and irregular temporal observations, which limit their direct use for operational groundwater status assessment. Mediterranean groundwater systems are subject to strong seasonal contrasts between winter recharge and summer abstraction, yet national-scale assessments resolving how aquifer type modulates this signal remain scarce. We analyzed 22,281 quality-controlled groundwater level records from 2,477 monitoring wells across the 14 River Basin Districts of Greece (2013 to 2022), drawn from the WISE database of the European Environment Agency, combining stratified non-parametric statistics with an interpretable XGBoost classification framework for screening of deeper-than-normal groundwater conditions. Seasonal dynamics differed systematically by aquifer type (Kruskal-Wallis H = 32.37, p = 9.34 × 10 −8 ). Porous aquifers showed the smallest seasonal amplitude (σ = 5.36 m) and the strongest coupling with root-zone soil moisture (Spearman ρ = +0.228), consistent with diffuse vertical Darcian recharge. Karstic aquifers exhibited intermediate amplitude (σ = 6.42 m) with a marked elevation gradient in dry-season drawdown, from + 0.79 m at low elevation to + 2.83 m above 300 m, reflecting dual-porosity behaviour in upland carbonate massifs. Fractured-rock aquifers displayed the largest amplitude (σ = 6.83 m) and effectively no soil-moisture coupling (ρ = +0.020), consistent with preferential recharge bypassing the soil column. The divergence in soil-moisture sensitivity between porous and fractured systems is the clearest statistical contrast in the dataset and is consistent with a difference in dominant recharge pathway, although the observational design does not allow that mechanism to be established directly. Within porous aquifers, sites combining high cropland cover and high vegetation vigour showed net summer recovery (Δh = − 0.42 m, Mann-Whitney p = 2.79 × 10 −3 ), a signal consistent with irrigation return flow that was statistically absent in karstic and fractured systems (p > 0.3). Among wells with continuous records over 2018 to 2022, 61.7% showed net decline and 100 wells (6.8%) showed persistent drawdown above 2 m per measurement interval, concentrated in Thessaly and the Messara plain; with only five annual values and irregular observation intervals, these are reported as short-period changes among repeatedly monitored wells rather than as national depletion trends. A station-standardized XGBoost classifier achieved ROC AUC = 0.695 on an independent 2021 to 2022 test set, with SHAP attribution identifying seasonal phase, antecedent soil moisture, annual precipitation, and potential evapotranspiration as the leading physically coherent predictors. The findings support consideration of aquifer-type-stratified reference conditions within the Water Framework Directive and provide a quantitative basis for prioritising monitoring investments in karstic and fractured-rock systems.

title: Human proximity to rivers in China
abstract: River proximity shapes human settlement patterns and water resource dependence, yet the long-term changes of human–river proximity and their drivers remain poorly understood. Using high-resolution population data for ten reference years, we developed a Proximity to Rivers Index (PRI) to quantify changes in population-density gradients relative to major rivers across China from 1953 to 2020. Random Forest models and counterfactual scenarios were used to examine socio-economic and natural associations with PRI. Despite a doubling of the population, the median population–river distance remained close to 10 km. However, PRI became progressively more negative from 1953 to 2020, indicating strengthening population concentration near rivers without a substantial shift in the median population location. Basin-scale trajectories were heterogeneous: human–river proximity generally strengthened in northern basins, whereas several southern basins exhibited weakening or more complex trends. Socio-economic variables were more strongly associated with the long-term PRI change, particularly in northern basins, while natural variability was more closely related to fluctuations among reference years in several southern basins. Urbanization rate and GDP had the highest relative importance nationally. Urban settlements were consistently closer to rivers than rural settlements, whereas the relationship between per-capita GDP and river proximity varied among Eastern, Central, and Western China. These findings highlight the need for basin-specific management that coordinates urban development, river-corridor protection, water-resource allocation, and climate adaptation.
